Benchmarks

Pointe Conversational Engineering Benchmarks

Five benchmarks of conversational engineering, measuring what a voice layer costs a coding agent. The agent is held fixed, and the same tasks reach it typed or spoken, so a score is the loss the voice interface adds, not the strength of the agent. Pointe is the system under test. The flagship is Humanity's Last Keystroke: small coding tasks, finished by voice only.

First run 2026-11-23. Agent claude-haiku-5-5 in Claude Code 2.1.330. Synthetic speech in four Kokoro voices. Every number on this page is computed from raw rows committed in the repository.

  • A self-evaluation. Not a leaderboard. One system under test and reference arms written by Pointe's team, who know Pointe's internals. No outside product is tested.
  • Synthetic speech. Clean Kokoro voices, also Pointe's local voice. Results are an upper bound for every arm.
  • Small samples. Intervals are wide. Where they overlap, no ranking is claimed.
  • Reproducible. Each benchmark is frozen with its harness, items, audio hashes and the Pointe commit it measured.

Pointe against the LLM router

In this first run Pointe scored below the LLM router wherever an interval excludes zero. The findings under each benchmark say what drove the gap, including the parts that are bugs in Pointe and the parts that are biases of the benchmark. Spoken Actions has no paired row: its false-approval counts are too small and unstable to rank.

Unit: task family (12 families, 36 tasks)

Humanity's Last Keystroke (HLK)

Is a small scripted coding task finished by voice only, when the keyboard version is finished?

36 tasks in 12 families; two runs per paid armRuns hlk-20261123-040919, hlk-20261123-085104, 2026-11-23Agent claude-haiku-5-5 in Claude Code 2.1.330, acceptEditsPointe 6544cdc (frozen before the first paid row), default setupLLM router brain anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5

  • Keyboard, canonical minus Pointe: +50 points (+31 to +69), paired by family.
  • Keyboard, canonical minus LLM router: +11 points (-1 to +31).
  • Pointe minus LLM router: -39 points (-62 to -15).
  • In 33 of Pointe's 38 failed runs a spoken yes did not take (Pointe asks for a tap on a request it cannot read out) and the voice-only scripted user then said no. That counts runs, not causes: in 24 of them the agent changed no file; in the other 9 it had already written code that failed, often because Pointe passed on a wrong instruction.
  • Known biases against Pointe: a timing race in the scripted user left some of its agents' follow-up questions unanswered, and one item (spelled-out seed 2) does not say the case it scores.

Passes over runs (synthetic speech). Runs of one task are not independent: read the paired gaps.

Unit: target symbol

Spoken Identifiers

When a symbol in the repository is spoken, does the agent change the right one and nothing else?

24 targets, each spoken in a clean and a 12 dB babble clipRuns identifiers-20261123-031106, identifiers-20261123-040357 (the LLM router arm rerun in full after a harness fix), 2026-11-23Agent claude-haiku-5-5 in Claude Code 2.1.330, acceptEditsPointe 6544cdc; one recognizer for every speech arm (soniox:stt-rt-v6)LLM router claude-sonnet-5-5; voices af_heart, am_michael, bf_emma, bm_george

  • Pointe minus LLM router: -2 points (-10 to +6); Pointe minus keyword rules: -6 points (-17 to +2). No speech arm is measurably better than another.
  • Pointe minus keyboard, canonical: -17 points (-29 to -6); Pointe typed minus Pointe spoken: +17 points (+6 to +29). Speech costs Pointe something; its text path does not.
  • Pointe right on 22/24 clean clips and 18/24 under 12 dB babble (the clean and babble clips use different voices).
  • Flip rate on repeated clips: Pointe 1/12, LLM router 3/12.
  • Main failures: the write/right homophone in every speech arm, and misheard words that Pointe and the LLM router rewrote as code names the agent could not find, where keyword rules passed the words as heard.

Unit: utterance

Spoken Actions and False Approval

Does speech become the right harness action, and how often does something that is not a yes approve a destructive prompt?

120 utterances; 60 adversarial non-yes on destructive prompts, 20 clear yesRun act-20261123-033255, 2026-11-23, 450 rowsAgent claude-haiku-5-5 in Claude Code 2.1.330, permission mode defaultPointe 6544cdc, default setupLLM router anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5, with a prompt we wrote that names the adversarial types

  • Outside the 8 truncated clips, Pointe and the LLM router both approved 0/52 and 0/52 non-yes utterances. Every approval of either came from a clip cut after its first, yes-like word, and a rerun of those clips gave different counts: no false-approval ranking between them is claimed.
  • Pointe's false denials: 3/13 on voice-readable prompts; the rest are commands Pointe never approves by voice and asks a tap for.
  • Missed stop: Pointe 8/8: at this commit it has no interrupt for Claude Code.
  • Pointe's accuracy is 92/120 if denying a hedge counted as correct.
  • In 3 runs Pointe's spoken reply claimed an approval, rejection or stop that did not happen.

Unit: conversation

Session Routing

With four live sessions, does a spoken request reach the right one, and is an ambiguous one asked about?

12 conversations of 5 turns (60 turns)Run routing-20261123-0331-d17a, 2026-11-23Agent claude-haiku-5-5 in Claude Code 2.1.330, acceptEditsPointe 6544cdc: brain anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5, ears soniox, mouth elevenlabs:eleven_v4_turboLLM router claude-sonnet-5-5 at effort low; ears soniox:stt-rt-v6

  • Pointe minus LLM router, paired by turn: -23 points (-32 to -15) (bootstrap by conversation).
  • In 9 of Pointe's 19 failed turns its brain chose the right session and words, and its send layer delivered an earlier request's text instead (7 right after it asked which session). This is a real bug; the benchmark's one-template sentences trigger it far more often than varied speech would, so the gap is overstated.
  • Had those sends gone out as the brain wrote them, Pointe would reach at most 50/60: an upper bound, not measured, still below the LLM router.
  • Flip rate on 3 repeated conversations: Pointe 2/15, LLM router 1/15 (not like for like: the router reuses cached transcripts).

Run it on your harness

Any conversational harness that can take audio or text and drive a coding agent can be measured.

  1. Get the repository and check it, free. No keys, no spend. 
    git clone https://github.com/ballerine-io/pointe.git && cd pointe
uv sync --locked --extra local
uv run --locked --extra local python bench/conversational/hlk/run.py corpus
uv run --locked --extra local python bench/conversational/hlk/run.py verify
  2. Write an adapter. It receives the same audio at real-time pace (or the same text) and reports what it delivered, approved, stopped or said. The agent is started for you with the same launch line as every other arm, in a throwaway repository under /tmp. An item that needs something your harness lacks is shown as coverage, never as a failure.

    Each benchmark keeps the harness it was run with.

    BenchmarkIts harnessRegister the adapter in
    Humanity's Last Keystroke (HLK)bench/conversational/hlk/core/runner.py: make_adapter
    Spoken Identifiersbench/conversational/identifiers/identifiers/bench.py: make_adapter
    Spoken Actions and False Approvalbench/conversational/actions/run.py: adapter_for
    Session Routingbench/conversational/routing/run.py: make_arm
    Barge-in and Time to a Correct Answerbench/conversational/bargein/bargein/bench.py: make_adapter
  3. Smoke, then the full run. The runner checks a spend ledger before every launch and stops at the budget. Keys come from the macOS Keychain or the environment, into the one process that needs them. 
    uv run --locked --extra local python bench/conversational/hlk/run.py hlk --adapter yours --smoke
uv run --locked --extra local python bench/conversational/hlk/run.py hlk --adapter yours --budget-usd 55
  4. Report and share. run.py report recomputes every table from the rows. Send the rows and the adapter as a pull request; a better LLM router prompt is welcome too.
